analysis.one_liner: Cuts acid-rain pollution from power plants and funds cleaner coal technology.
analysis.headline: The bill never reached a House vote: after six subcommittee hearings in fall 1989, its action trail was closed in May 1990 with a pointer to H.R. 3030, the broader Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required states to phase in deep cuts in sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide from coal- and oil-burning power plants and major factories — a 10-million-ton sulfur dioxide goal — by 2004, with state plans, continuous emissions monitoring, limited emissions trading, and penalties that utilities could not pass on to electric customers. It also authorized up to $300 million a year in federal grants to demonstrate clean coal technology at existing plants and barred power companies from terminating existing coal supply contracts because of the new rules. It never got a vote; the House eventually handled acid rain in H.R. 3030 instead.
analysis.who_benefits: People living where acid rain falls — Northeast lakes, forests, and buildings — and anyone breathing sulfur dioxide pollution, since the bill mandates large emission cuts and requires utilities to install monitors and open their emissions records to the public. Coal-mining communities also gain, because the bill protects existing coal supply contracts from termination specifically to prevent miner unemployment, and clean-coal technology firms gain a federally funded demonstration market.

how_it_helps.text: Requires phased nationwide cuts of 10 million tons of sulfur dioxide and 3 million tons of nitrogen oxides, with statewide emissions-rate limits (1.2 pounds of sulfur dioxide per million Btu) due by the end of 2003, plus state plans the EPA must approve or reject within 12 months.

Makes every fossil-fuel power unit install continuous emissions monitoring and requires owners to keep emissions and operating records available to the EPA, so pollution can actually be verified rather than estimated.

Imposes per-pound noncompliance penalties on utilities that exceed their limits and explicitly forbids including those penalty costs in the rates charged to electric customers, putting the burden on shareholders instead of ratepayers.

Authorizes up to $300 million a year for fiscal 1990–1993 in federal grants, capped at 50% of project cost, to demonstrate clean coal technology at existing plants, with priority to the lowest cost per ton of pollution removed.
Prohibits early termination of pre-existing fossil fuel supply contracts due to the new rules, a provision written, in the bill's own words, to prevent unemployment of coal miners.

analysis.who_pays: Coal- and oil-burning utilities and their shareholders bear the compliance costs — scrubbers, cleaner fuel, monitoring — and face per-pound penalties they cannot pass through to customers. Electric customers would still absorb some compliance costs through rates (the bill only shields penalty costs from rates, not the price of installing controls). Taxpayers fund the clean coal grants, up to $1.2 billion over four years, and high-sulfur coal producers face shrinking demand as plants cut sulfur.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal-burning utilities, electric customers, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Only penalty costs are barred from electric rates; ordinary compliance costs (scrubbers, fuel switching) could still be recovered from customers, so households would pay part of the cleanup through higher electricity bills.

The bill funnels up to $300 million a year of federal money into keeping coal burning at existing plants, and exempts subsidized projects from the Clean Air Act's new-source performance standards — public money propping up the very fuel the bill is curbing.

Limits are set as statewide average emission rates rather than hard tonnage caps, so an individual plant could keep polluting heavily as long as cleaner plants elsewhere in the state offset it on paper.

The clean-coal program lets states extend a source's compliance deadline by up to two years, and excuses statewide shortfalls caused by failed clean-coal projects, softening the enforcement the bill's title promises.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core mandate — a 10-million-ton sulfur dioxide cut with monitoring, verification, and penalties that hit shareholders rather than ratepayers — was a genuine public-health and environmental gain, and the later 1990 law showed large acid-rain reductions were achievable. But the bill hedges in favor of coal: federal subsidies for clean coal, an exemption from new-source standards for subsidized projects, two-year compliance extensions, and contract-termination protections. The statewide rate-averaging design is weaker than the tonnage-based trading system Congress actually adopted in 1990. A fair reading: real cleanup, purchased partly with public money, and softer enforcement than advertised.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee — six subcommittee hearings in fall 1989, no markup, no floor vote — and in May 1990 the House closed its action trail by pointing to H.R. 3030, the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990, which became law that November.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Bilirakis introduced the bill on June 8, 1989, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce; one Republican colleague signed on as cosponsor.

The bill was assigned to two subcommittees, on Health and the Environment and on Energy and Power, which held six hearings between September 7 and October 19, 1989, but the full committee never voted to send it to the floor.

On May 23, 1990, the action record was closed with the note 'For Further Action See H.R. 3030' — the broader Clean Air Act reauthorization that Congress passed and President George H.W. Bush signed into law in November 1990, which settled acid rain with a nationwide emissions-allowance trading program rather than this bill's state-by-state rate limits.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people ultimately got the acid-rain reductions anyway, through H.R. 3030. Coal-burning utilities also came out ahead, because the 1990 law let them trade emission allowances nationwide instead of meeting this bill's rigid per-state rate mandates with penalties they could not pass to customers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public, via the 1990 Clean Air Act; utilities too

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken on the bill; its sponsor and its single cosponsor were both Republicans, and the record shows no organized opposition, so the partisan shape of the fight cannot be read from the record.

industries.note: They would bear most compliance costs, install continuous monitoring, open their emissions records, and face per-pound penalties barred from passing to customers. Their access to 50% federal cost-sharing for clean coal retrofits only partially offsets that burden.

The bill cuts demand for high-sulfur coal by forcing sulfur out of power plant fuel, but it also locks coal in: it protects existing coal supply contracts from termination to prevent miner unemployment, requires subsidized projects to burn US-mined coal, and spends federal money on technology to keep existing coal plants running.

Federal grants capped at 50% of project cost plus the retrofit mandate create a market for scrubbers and cleaner combustion technology; the bill requires the technology to cost no more than conventional controls.
